title: More Than One Blow
paragraphs: The extinction of the non-bird dinosaurs about sixty-six million years ago is often told as a single dramatic event: a giant asteroid strikes, and an age ends. The Natural History Museum in London supports the impact theory, locating the crater on the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico, but it also stresses that the last dinosaurs lived in a world already undergoing environmental change. Some of those changes began millions of years before the impact, which makes the asteroid the final blow rather than the sole cause.

Not every researcher agrees on emphasis. An article from the United States National Science Foundation argues that the climate upheavals following the impact did most of the killing, rather than the blast itself. An international panel of scientists, reporting in twenty ten, concluded by contrast that the impact was the best explanation for the extinction. Researchers at the American Museum of Natural History add that some paleontologists believe dinosaurs were already declining before the asteroid struck. These positions differ less in the facts they accept than in the weight they give to each stage of a chain of events.

What is beyond dispute, however, is that extinction was not total. Birds are living dinosaurs, the descendants of one branch of the theropods, and their ancestors survived the catastrophe. The same event that ended one dynasty of large animals therefore opened the ecological space for others, including the mammals from which we descend. Understanding extinction thus means understanding not only what was lost, but what became possible afterwards. The question of proportion may never be settled completely, but the broad outline is remarkably well supported.
